messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Markus Weber is a 49-year-old city council member who came to treatment after months of telling his wife that he was “fine” and then startling so violently in bed when she reached for his shoulder that she began sleeping more cautiously beside him. He had served in combat years earlier, and when he speaks about the event he still does so in fragments. He remembers being in a convoy and then being on the ground after an explosion, with sound dropping in and out and pieces of the scene coming back without order: dust, shouting, a body too close to him, the sense that he was about to die. What remains most vivid is the terror. When he tries to explain the sequence clearly, he loses the thread, stops mid-sentence, and looks as if he is back there rather than describing it from a distance. The gaps in his memory have taken on meaning for him. Because he can only recall parts of what happened and cannot form a complete account, he has come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that his own body cannot be trusted, as if it knows he is under threat before his mind does.

That belief has shaped the way he lives now. Markus is certain that safety is always provisional, something people say to comfort themselves but not something that can be relied on. Even in familiar settings, including council chambers and public meetings he has attended for years, he feels he has to stay on guard. He scans the room automatically, tracks movement in the doorway, and notices who is behind him. When colleagues or constituents reach out to greet him with a hand on the arm or shoulder, he reacts with immediate alarm, his whole body jerking before he can think. The reaction itself frightens him. He has come to see these bodily surges as further proof that his body is working against him, still acting as though the danger is present, and each episode leaves him more convinced that the world really is as unsafe as he feels it to be.

The memories and the threat responses feed each other. At night, when he lies awake unable to settle into sleep, bits of the combat scene intrude more forcefully: the missing pieces remain missing, but the terror arrives intact. On those nights he can feel his body bracing in the dark, listening for sounds in the house, unable to accept his wife’s reassurance that they are safe at home. And after days when he has been especially keyed up—after a crowded council session, or an unexpected touch in a hallway—the memory becomes even less coherent when he tries to think about it, more like shards than a story, with the same original fear rushing back and cutting off his ability to speak.

Over time Markus has developed ways of managing that he experiences as necessary. When images or bodily fear begin to rise, he turns on loud television or music to drown out his own thoughts. He also monitors his mind closely, watching for any sign that he might be “going crazy,” as he puts it, especially when he feels himself losing the thread while remembering. He avoids physical contact whenever he can, sidestepping embraces at public events and keeping a careful distance even from people he likes. In the moment these habits give him something to do, but they also keep him from staying with the memory long enough for it to become clearer. The event remains patchy and unspeakable, and because it remains that way, it continues to return charged with terror rather than as something finished and past.

Those same strategies have deepened his sense that something is wrong with him. The more he orchestrates his day around preventing contact, controlling noise, and checking his own mind for signs of collapse, the more he experiences himself as a man whose body is unpredictable and whose surroundings require constant vigilance. In his work this has become increasingly visible. He now prefers the edge seat in meetings, keeps people out of his personal space during constituent events, and leaves some receptions early because the press of bodies feels intolerable. At home, his wife has experienced him as distant and tense, especially because even ordinary touch can set off an alarmed reaction he cannot hide.

What finally brought him in was not a single flashback or a single bad night, but the recognition that his life had narrowed around staying prepared. He was exhausted from poor sleep, ashamed of recoiling from touch, and increasingly unable to give a straightforward account of the combat event without feeling overwhelmed by the same terror. What frightens him most is the idea that this constant watchfulness means he will never really feel safe again; what he hopes, more quietly, is that he might learn how to be at home in his body and with his wife without bracing for danger.
